query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by temperature‐induced surface segregation of the lower‐melting component (copper). As heating increases, copper atoms preferentially migrate toward the nanoparticle surfaces to form a copper-rich, liquid-like shell that initiates premelting below the overall bulk melting temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, equiatomic iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with a statistically homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled comparison between baseline HEA nanoparticles and a modified batch in which surface segregation is inhibited (for example, by applying an ultrathin inert coating that minimizes copper diffusion).
generation.conditions: Heating experiments conducted in situ (e.g., via high-resolution TEM) over the range from near 0.9Tm to above the melting onset, with identical particle size distributions (typically below ~10 nm in diameter) and under identical atmosphere and heating rates.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a copper-enriched surface layer that is liquid-like at temperatures below the melting point of the core alloy.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the relatively lower surface energy and melting point of copper drive its thermally activated migration to the nanoparticle surface. This segregation lowers the effective surface melting temperature, leading first to the premelting of the surface region, which then propagates inward with further heating.
generation.predicted_outcome: Baseline nanoparticles (with unmodified surfaces) will show signs of premelting—such as formation of a liquid-like surface layer, morphological softening, or local melting—at a lower temperature compared to nanoparticles where copper segregation is suppressed by an inert coating. In the latter, the onset of surface melting will be delayed, and the overall melting transition will more closely resemble that of a chemically homogeneous particle.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic HEA nanoparticles without any intervention, exhibiting natural copper surface segregation upon heating.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles of sizes where surface effects are dominant (typically <10 nm) and in HEA systems where at least one constituent (copper) has a significantly lower melting point and surface energy relative to the other components.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature offset between the premelting onset in modified versus baseline particles and the quantitative extent of the copper surface enrichment remain uncertain, as they may depend on particle size distribution, specific interfacial energies, and kinetic factors not entirely characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of equiatomic iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles. One group serves as the baseline, while the other is coated with an ultrathin inert layer known to impede surface diffusion. Subject both groups to identical in situ heating experiments (using high-resolution TEM with EDS mapping) across the premelting regime.
measurements: Onset temperature of surface premelting determined from morphological changes (e.g., rounding or softening of the surface)
Surface elemental composition (especially copper concentration) via spatially resolved EDS
Overall melting temperature of the nanoparticles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If baseline nanoparticles do not exhibit a copper-rich, liquid-like surface layer prior to full melting or if the inertly coated nanoparticles do not display a higher onset temperature for premelting compared to baseline particles, then the hypothesis that copper surface segregation controls the premelting/melting behavior will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Do high-entropy nanoalloys exhibit the theoretically predicted sluggish diffusion and enhanced thermal stability, or do they undergo phase separation and structural evolution at high temperatures?. System: AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy nanoalloys (HENA), specifically near-equimolar compositions (≈Au20Co28Cu11Ni20Pt21) with diameters of 3–6.5 nm.. Processing: Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) on amorphous 50 nm SiN membranes or 5 nm carbon films; substrate temperature 873 K, laser frequency 5 Hz, total nominal thickness 4 nm.. Test conditions: In situ aberration-corrected STEM heating from 298 to 973 K (steps at 473, 673, 773, 873, 973 K) with a heating rate of 1 K s⁻¹; MD simulations from 400 to 1500 K using EAM potentials.. Findings: Particle size distribution remains unchanged at 473 K but widens up to 13 nm at 973 K due to coalescence of smallest NPs (2–4 nm).; NPs reshape from elliptical to spherical shapes as the in-plane shape ratio increases with temperature.; Phase separation occurs progressively with temperature, driven by the segregation of Au and Cu to the NP surface.; At 973 K, a complete loss of gold and copper is observed due to the melting and evaporation
